did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title identifies it as a maskil of David—a psalm of reflection—and connects David’s prayer with a time when he was in a cave. The title itself does not specify which cave it was.

Did you know? The psalm begins with repetition: “I cry aloud to the LORD; I plead aloud to the LORD.” This repetition emphasizes the intensity of the cry and its movement from calling out to pleading.

Did you know? The psalmist describes his prayer as his “lament,” which he pours out before the LORD. In other words, he openly brings his troubles and pain before Him, without concealing his condition.

Did you know? Even when the psalmist’s spirit grows faint—“when my spirit grows weak within me”—he holds on to the knowledge that the LORD knows his path. The same verse also mentions the danger: enemies have hidden a trap for him along the way he travels.

Did you know? The psalm’s description of loneliness is especially stark: the psalmist looks to his right and finds no one who knows him, no refuge, and no one concerned for him. The verse presents not only external danger but also a complete absence of human support.

Did you know? In the face of losing every human refuge, the psalmist declares, “You are my refuge, my portion.” The LORD is described here both as a place of protection and as the person’s portion “in the land of the living.”

Did you know? The psalmist asks the LORD to listen to his cry even though he is “brought very low,” explaining that he needs rescue because his persecutors are too strong for him. Thus, the prayer combines an acknowledgment of weakness with a direct appeal for help.

Did you know? The purpose of rescue is not merely to escape distress: the psalmist asks to be brought out of prison so that he can give thanks to the LORD. He also expects the righteous to surround him with joy when the LORD deals generously with him and saves him.
